proposals.stanceName: One Color, One Verb — a fixed global grammar where each button is a word learned once
proposals.inputGrammar:
FIVE WORDS, LEARNED ONCE. Physical-order assumption (FLAGGED): single row under the screen in bitfield order GRAY | YELLOW | GREEN | BLUE | RED, GREEN center. The grammar depends on YELLOW sitting left of GREEN and BLUE right of it; if the case order differs, the prev/next pair must be remapped before the grammar is frozen.

FRAMEWORK-OWNED (apps can never rebind):
- GRAY press = SYSTEM. Toggles the Home overlay (breadcrumb, help/legend, app menu items, "Exit to App Explorer"). Works on every screen including fullscreen canvas/games.
- GRAY long (1 s) = eject: exit straight to App Explorer, no menu.
- RED press = BACK/CANCEL. Pops one screen or closes the topmost dialog. On the app's root screen it exits to App Explorer. Mashing RED from anywhere always lands you home — this is a framework invariant, not an app choice.
- RED long = RESERVED. ~6 s is hardware power-off (FwOGapp contract); the default power policy draws a shutdown countdown from ~2 s so a user mashing "back" who holds too long sees what is about to happen. Nothing is ever parked on long-RED.

FIXED APP VERBS (one meaning per verb everywhere; only how the widget renders it varies):
- YELLOW press = PREVIOUS (up a list row, page left, decrement a value). Hold = auto-repeat, 10 Hz after 400 ms (the BSP phase machine's down_since_ms gives this for free).
- BLUE press = NEXT (down a list row, page right, increment). Hold = auto-repeat.
- GREEN press = GO (select the highlighted row, OK a dialog, advance the story, start the thing). The universal "yes".
- GREEN long (600 ms) = ACTION — the ONE app-definable slot in the whole grammar. It must be registered with a text label, which the footer legend displays (e.g. "Pause", "Shuffle"); unlabeled = no-op. This is the entire contextual budget; everything else is forbidden.

No double-press, no chords: five verbs plus one labeled long-press is the whole language.
proposals.screenAnatomy:
320x240 landscape, three fixed bands (framework draws bands 1 and 3; apps only ever own band 2):

1. STATUS BAR — y 0–19 (320x20): app name left (≤120 px), current screen title / breadcrumb tail center, indicators (battery, IR, BLE) right 60 px. Answers "where am I" at all times.
2. CONTENT — y 20–203 (320x184): the app's canvas. List widget: 6 rows at 28 px + selection highlight. Text page: 11 lines of 2x-scaled lcd_text (~16 px). Value editor: 48 px big-number center with unit. Canvas screens get the full 320x184.
3. KEY LEGEND — y 204–239 (320x36): five 64x36 keycaps rendered in the physical button order, each filled with its button's color plus a glyph and 1–2 word label of what that verb does RIGHT NOW ("Menu | Prev | Select | Next | Back"). This footer is the live manual — the zero-manual learnability mechanism. Labels + position carry meaning redundantly with color (colorblind-safe).

OVERLAY (GRAY) — 260x180 card centered over dimmed content: full breadcrumb path ("wilidoro > settings > theme"), Resume, app-registered menu items, Exit to App Explorer.
FULLSCREEN MODE (games/canvas) — app may collapse bands 1+3 to a 12 px hint strip ("GRAY = menu"); GRAY and RED remain framework-owned so fullscreen never becomes a trap.
components: StatusBar — always-on top band: app name, screen title, system indicators
KeyLegend — five color-matched footer keycaps showing each verb's current label; auto-updates per screen
List — vertical menu, YELLOW/BLUE move highlight (hold to repeat-scroll), GREEN selects, 6 visible rows with scroll indicator
Pager — horizontal page carousel with dot indicator; YELLOW/BLUE turn pages (story browser, wizards)
ValueEditor — big-number spinner with unit label; YELLOW/BLUE step (hold accelerates), GREEN commits, RED cancels
ToggleRow — list row variant that flips on GREEN
ConfirmDialog — modal card, GREEN = yes, RED = no; the only two buttons it listens to
Toast — 2 s bottom-edge notice above the legend, no input
TextPage — lcd_text reader with page position indicator; YELLOW/BLUE page
BigStat — huge center readout (timer digits, score) for canvas-lite screens
HomeOverlay — the GRAY system card: breadcrumb, help, app menu items, exit (framework-owned)
Canvas — raw gfx escape hatch for games; app draws band 2, framework still owns GRAY/RED and the legend
FeedbackKit — standard non-screen echo: nav tick + confirm chime + descending exit tone on I2S, WS2812 strip as 7-step progress/position bar
proposals.exitStory: Three redundant, framework-guaranteed answers to "where am I and how do I leave" — none of which an app can disable: (1) the status bar always shows app name + screen title, and the footer legend's RED cap always reads "Back" (or "Exit" on the root screen); (2) RED is a hardware-truth escape: every press pops one level, and the screen stack bottoms out in App Explorer, so mashing RED from any depth — including a game's fullscreen canvas — always gets out (the orca-field-notes trap becomes impossible because nav events never reach app code); (3) GRAY from anywhere raises the system overlay with the full breadcrumb and an explicit "Exit to App Explorer" item, and long-GRAY jumps there directly. Safety rail on the one collision: since a panicking user may hold RED, the default power policy paints a shutdown countdown from ~2 s of hold so power-off is never a surprise.
proposals.resourcePlan: Bespoke micro-toolkit (fwui) on top of the BSP's existing lcd_text renderer + graphics LCD API — NOT LVGL. Rationale: LVGL costs ~390 KB flash and 143 KB of the display CPU's 264 KB RAM; a mandatory framework that eats 54% of RAM before the app draws a pixel forbids exactly the feature work this system exists to enable. fwui's widget set is deliberately tiny (13 components above) and renders band-by-band with partial redraw — no retained full framebuffer (a full 320x240x16 frame is 153 KB and stays off the table). Budget: ~24–32 KB flash and ≤10 KB RAM for the framework (screen stack, legend state, one 320x28 row strip buffer, dirty rects), i.e. roughly the cost of today's bare display app plus a rounding error. Flash is a non-issue (16 MB). LVGL stays in the BSP as an opt-in for showcase apps like ogvegas that want its widget depth and can pay 143 KB; fwui is the default that `fw new-app` scaffolds against, and its input layer feeds the same debounced phase state machine, so the two coexist.
risks: Physical layout assumption: the grammar requires YELLOW left of GREEN and BLUE right of it (bitfield order on a single row). If the case arranges buttons differently, prev/next will feel inverted — verify against real hardware before freezing the grammar.

Games get only 2 nav + GREEN + one long-press: a 4-direction game (like the current LVGL demo's D-pad mapping) cannot exist under the fixed grammar. Escape valve is the IMU (tilt = analog 2-axis, already proven by wilidoro's tilt-to-pause); if that proves insufficient, the pressure to grant a grammar exemption for a 'game mode' is the stance's biggest long-term threat.

RED back vs 6 s RED power-off share a button: mitigated by the 2 s countdown overlay, but an untested user mashing-then-holding in a panic is a real path to accidental shutdown — needs a hallway test.
Bespoke toolkit = maintenance burden the LVGL ecosystem would have carried (fonts, RTL, future widgets). Mitigation is a frozen component list; scope creep toward 'tiny LVGL' erases the RAM win.
Color-is-meaning fails for red/green colorblind users; the legend must always carry position + glyph + text, never color alone, and this needs to be a lint/review rule not a hope.

Migration debt: ogvegas, orca field notes, and the LVGL demo all speak the old UP/LEFT/RIGHT/DOWN/ENTER keypad dialect; until retrofitted, the fleet teaches two contradictory grammars, which is worse for learnability than either alone.
proposals.pitch: Five buttons, five words, learned once: GRAY is the system, YELLOW/BLUE step backward/forward, GREEN says yes, RED retreats — and holding RED long enough retreats all the way to off, which makes even the hardware power contract rhyme with the grammar. Because the framework owns GRAY and RED unconditionally, "how do I get out" has a hardware-guaranteed answer on every screen ever shipped, and the always-visible color-matched legend under the screen is a live manual that makes the device self-teaching in one session. Apps are declared, not drawn — a real 3-screen feature is ~30 lines against fwui's stack-of-screens API, with navigation, exit, power, legend, chimes, and the LED strip all inherited — and at ≤10 KB RAM instead of LVGL's 143 KB, the framework leaves the display CPU to the feature. The 5-button constraint stops being a limitation and becomes the product's accent: every FreeWili app speaks the same five-color language, so shipping the tenth app costs a fraction of the first and the user already knows how to drive it before it's flashed.

components: fwui_statusbar — framework-owned top strip: app name + screen title + registered icons; apps cannot remove it
fwui_hintbar — framework-owned bottom strip of 5 color chips (physical button order) auto-labeled with each button's current meaning; the zero-manual mechanism
fwui_list — vertical focus list (GRAY/RED move, GREEN select); auto-scrollbar, 7 visible rows, repeat-scroll
fwui_menu — fwui_list of actions with callbacks; the default screen type
fwui_grid — 2D icon/tile grid; all four directions move focus, GREEN activates
fwui_pager — horizontal page carousel (YELLOW/BLUE), dot indicator in hint-bar row
fwui_spinner — numeric editor: YELLOW/BLUE step value, GREEN commits; min/max/step declared
fwui_choice — enum cycler (YELLOW/BLUE through options), same shape as spinner
fwui_textview — scrollable read-only text (GRAY/RED with repeat); powers orca-style story browsing
fwui_dialog — modal yes/no: hint bar recolors to YELLOW=No GREEN=Yes; used by the built-in exit confirm
fwui_progress — bar in content area, optional mirror onto the 7-LED WS2812 strip (wilidoro-style ring)
fwui_toast — timed banner overlay (also used by the RED-hold power-off countdown)
fwui_ctxmenu — LONG-GREEN overlay listing app-registered actions; framework always appends 'Exit to App Explorer' as the last item
fwui_nav (invisible) — the back stack: fwui_push/fwui_pop, LONG-YELLOW pops, empty stack triggers exit dialog
proposals.exitStory: A lost user has four concentric answers, all framework-owned so no app can remove them. (1) WHERE AM I: the status bar (top 20px) always shows app name + screen title — every screen, no exceptions. (2) ONE STEP BACK: the yellow hint chip always reads 'hold: Back' when the back stack is non-empty; LONG-YELLOW pops one screen, everywhere. (3) ALL THE WAY OUT: at the root screen the yellow chip reads 'hold: Exit', and LONG-YELLOW opens the framework's 'Exit to App Explorer?' dialog (YELLOW=No, GREEN=Yes). Redundantly, the LONG-GREEN context menu always ends with 'Exit to App Explorer' — two independent paths out, both labeled on-screen in the button's own color. (4) LAST RESORT: hold RED — at 3s the framework paints a 'Powering off in 3…2…1' toast so the 6s hardware cutoff is announced, not mysterious. The orca-field-notes incident becomes impossible: the exit affordance is painted on every frame by the framework, not opted into by the app.
proposals.inputGrammar: GLOBAL, identical in every app. PRESS (release <700ms): GRAY=UP/focus-prev, YELLOW=LEFT/prev-page/decrement, GREEN=ENTER/select, BLUE=RIGHT/next-page/increment, RED=DOWN/focus-next — exactly the existing BSP LVGL keypad map, now a contract. REPEAT: only the vertical pair auto-repeats (GRAY/RED held >500ms → 8Hz, accelerating to 20Hz after 2s, so a 200-item list never needs a 6s hold). YELLOW/BLUE deliberately do NOT repeat — that frees them for long-press without gesture collision. LONG (700ms, fires once): LONG-YELLOW = BACK (global, framework-handled; pops the back stack; at root opens the exit dialog — 'left = back' matches every UI convention on earth). LONG-GREEN = context menu overlay (contextual, app-registered actions; framework always appends 'Exit to App Explorer'). LONG-GRAY and LONG-BLUE = reserved, unbound (BLUE already means display-bootloader at boot; keep it clean). LONG-RED = FORBIDDEN to apps — the framework API refuses to bind it, because ~6s RED is hardware power-off; instead, RED held past 3s triggers a framework countdown toast ('Powering off…') turning the reserved gesture into a visible feature rather than a trap. Contextual remaps (e.g. dialog: YELLOW=No, GREEN=Yes) are allowed only for PRESS meanings and only when the hint bar displays the new label — the chip is the license to remap. ASSUMPTION THIS DEPENDS ON: buttons sit in a single row beneath the screen in bitfield order GRAY-YELLOW-GREEN-BLUE-RED left-to-right, which makes the grammar spatially self-evident (center=select, inner pair=left/right, outer pair=up/down) and lets hint chips align with physical buttons. If the real case order differs, one board-config table reorders the chips — but if buttons are NOT in a row (e.g. a diamond), the outer/inner logic should be re-derived before shipping.
proposals.pitch: This wins because it turns the 1-OG's oddest constraint — five differently-colored buttons — into its interface identity: color IS the label. One spatial grammar (the BSP's existing gray/yellow/green/blue/red = up/left/enter/right/down keypad map, promoted to a contract) drives every widget, so a user who learns one screen has learned every app ever written for the device; and the always-on hint bar paints each button's current meaning in that button's own color, 24px above the physical button itself, making the device literally self-documenting — zero manual, glance down, press the color you see. The two failure modes observed in the wild are closed by construction: 'how do I leave' is answered on every frame by framework-owned Back/Exit affordances no app can omit, and the RED-down-vs-RED-power collision is defused by an announced countdown. For developers it's ruthless leverage: the framework rides the LVGL port already in the BSP (focus groups, keypad indev, scrolling — solved problems), so a complete, navigable, exitable 3-screen feature is ~30 lines of declarative C with zero pixel math. Features get cranked out; UI comes for free.
proposals.resourcePlan: Build fwui as a thin layer (~15KB flash, ~2-4KB RAM) on the EXISTING LVGL 9 port — don't write a bespoke widget kit. Rationale by the numbers: 390KB flash is 2.4% of the display CPU's 16MB — irrelevant; 143KB RAM of 264KB leaves ~120KB free, and the display CPU's entire job is UI, so spending its RAM on UI is the correct allocation. LVGL already gives focus groups, the 5-button keypad indev, scrolling, styles, and invalidation-based partial redraw; a bespoke kit would be rebuilding those badly, and lcd_text alone can't do focus rings or smooth lists, which are the heart of the spatial stance. Configure LVGL with dual 320x24 partial draw buffers (~30KB, already inside the 143KB figure) and compile out unused widget classes to claw back flash/RAM if an app runs tight. lcd_text stays in the BSP untouched as the escape hatch for deliberately tiny non-fwui apps (~32KB class), but the framework targets LVGL only — two rendering backends in one framework is double maintenance for zero user value. Revisit only if a real app measurably exhausts the ~120KB headroom (large image assets are the likely culprit; the fix is flash-resident images via LVGL's direct-flash image decoder, not a new renderer).
risks: Button physical-layout assumption: the whole spatial story (outer=vertical, inner=horizontal, center=select) and hint-chip alignment assume a single row in bitfield order GRAY-YELLOW-GREEN-BLUE-RED under the screen. Verify against the actual case before freezing the grammar; a diamond or split layout demands re-derivation, not just a chip-reorder table.

RED double duty (DOWN + 6s power-off): accelerated repeat (20Hz after 2s) makes long RED holds unnecessary and the 3s countdown toast makes the cutoff visible, but a user mashing DOWN in a frozen app can still power off unexpectedly. Accepted; the countdown is the mitigation, and 6s-RED doubles as the escape from a hung app.

Color instinct vs spatial role: RED=DOWN fights the universal red=stop reflex (GREEN=go conveniently agrees with ENTER). The hint bar is the antidote — meaning is always painted — but expect early users to press RED hoping to cancel; watch for it in testing and lean on YELLOW-chip 'Back' visibility.

Text input is unsolved: 5 buttons + spatial grammar handles lists/values/pages well and text terribly. No text-entry component in v1; first app needing free text (wifi password, naming) forces a bespoke picker design.

RAM ceiling: ~120KB headroom after LVGL is fine for widget UIs but an image-heavy showcase app (ogvegas-class) could exhaust it; mitigation path is flash-resident image decoding, flagged in the resource plan.

CPU split ambiguity: if app logic runs on the main CPU while fwui/LVGL runs on the display CPU, every fwui_* call becomes IPC — latency, serialization, and API-shape risk. Pin down which CPU executes app code before finalizing the C API; the sketch assumes app code and fwui share a CPU.

Framework-owned chrome depends on the framework being alive: a busy-looping app stops hint-bar rendering and LONG-YELLOW handling. Consider a display-CPU watchdog that repaints an 'unresponsive — hold RED to power off' banner; not in v1.
proposals.screenAnatomy: 320x240 landscape, three fixed horizontal bands. STATUS BAR — y 0-19 (320x20): app name left-aligned (~120px, 12px font), screen title centered (~140px), up to 4 app-registered 16x16 icons right; framework-drawn every frame. CONTENT — y 20-215 (320x196): the app's declarative widgets live here; 8px side margins → 304px usable width; list rows 28px tall → 7 fully visible rows; focus ring is a 2px accent outline + row highlight. HINT BAR — y 216-239 (320x24): five chips of 60x20px with 4px gaps (5*60 + 4*4 + 2*2 edge = 316px), one per physical button in physical left-to-right order; each chip's background is its button's color with an auto-contrast label (10-12px) stating the button's CURRENT meaning (e.g. GRAY '▲', YELLOW '◀ / hold:Back', GREEN 'OK / hold:Menu', BLUE '▶', RED '▼'). Chips auto-populate from the focused widget type; apps may relabel via fwui_hint but may not hide the bar. Modal overlays (dialog, context menu) draw a centered panel of max 280x160 over dimmed content and retake the hint bar with their own chip labels. The 20/196/24 split is fixed — apps never position chrome, which is what makes every app look and steer the same.

proposals.stanceName: CHROMABAR — soft-key rail with a hard gray guarantee
proposals.inputGrammar:
PHYSICAL ASSUMPTION (FLAGGED): buttons are one row beneath the screen in hardware-bitfield order GRAY-YELLOW-GREEN-BLUE-RED, so a bottom on-screen rail aligns slot-to-button. If the case differs, the rail moves/reorders to stay physically aligned — verify the case before freezing geometry.

EVENT TYPES (built on fwog_btn_step/fwog_btn_held_ms):
- PRESS: if the slot has no long-binding, fires on down-edge (snappy). If it has a long-binding, fires on release before 600 ms.
- LONG: fires at 600 ms of settled hold (on threshold, not release). At 600 ms the slot flips to color-filled showing the long label + a short chime, so the user learns long meanings by accident, safely.
- REPEAT: only on bindings flagged REPEAT (scroll/adjust): first repeat at 400 ms, then 8 Hz while held.

GLOBAL (framework-owned, apps CANNOT rebind):
- GRAY press = Back (pop one screen). On the app's root screen, Back = exit to App Explorer (optional confirm if the app set a dirty flag).
- GRAY hold 1 s = Home: exit straight to App Explorer from ANY depth, even from raw-framebuffer "game mode" — the framework sits between the driver and the app and intercepts gray-hold unconditionally, drawing a filling "Home…" pill.
- RED hold: app sees red held only up to 1.5 s; past that the framework paints a "Keep holding to power off" pill and swallows the event until hardware cuts power at ~6 s. LONG-RED is therefore not bindable by apps, ever (collides with shutdown).
- GRAY long and RED long are the only reserved chords; everything else is contextual.

CONTEXTUAL (per screen, the rail labels ARE the manual):
- GREEN: primary/affirmative by convention (Select, OK, Start). Press + optional long.
- YELLOW / BLUE: the adjacent pair — prev/next, up/down, dec/inc in every stock component (with REPEAT). Freely rebindable on custom screens. Press + optional long each.
- RED: contextual press only — conventionally stop/cancel/delete (destructive family stays on the red button: color is meaning).
- An unbound slot renders a dim dot = "does nothing here", so silence is also labeled.
proposals.screenAnatomy:
320x240 landscape, three fixed regions (6x8 font at integer scales — 12x16 at scale 2, 18x24 at scale 3):

1. STATUS BAR — y 0..15 (320x16). Left: app/screen title, scale-2, up to ~20 chars. Right: breadcrumb depth dots (one filled dot per pushed screen, max 5 shown) + status glyphs (battery/IR/link). This bar answers "where am I" on every screen — title + depth dots, always drawn by the framework.

2. CONTENT — y 16..207 (320x192). The only region an app draws. Clean grids: 12 lines of scale-2 text (26 cols) or 8 lines of scale-3 (17 cols). Stock components own this region entirely; custom screens get a clipped gfx context for it.

3. SOFTKEY RAIL — y 208..239 (320x32). Five 64x32 slots, left-to-right GRAY/YELLOW/GREEN/BLUE/RED, each vertically above its physical button. Slot = centered label (scale-2, max 5 chars = 60 px of 64) + a 4 px underline bar in the button's color + 1 px separator. Pressed: slot inverts. Long threshold reached: slot fills solid with the button color, black long-label text. Gray slot always reads "Back" (or "Exit" on root); red slot dims and shows the power pill during a shutdown-length hold.

Toasts overlay y 184..207 (one scale-2 line above the rail) for 2 s; modals (Confirm) overlay the content region only — the rail stays, because the rail is the answer to the modal.
components: Rail — renders the 5 slots from the active screen's key table; handles press/long/repeat state, invert/fill feedback, and the reserved gray/red behavior; apps never draw it.
StatusBar — title + breadcrumb depth dots + status glyphs; framework-drawn on every push/pop.
List — scrolling menu: YELLOW/BLUE prev/next with repeat, GREEN select, GRAY back; scrollbar on right edge; the App-Explorer home screen and every app menu are this one component.
TextView — scrolling read-only text (orca field notes): YELLOW/BLUE scroll with repeat, optional GREEN action; shows N-of-M position in the status bar.
Pager — horizontal card carousel: YELLOW/BLUE page, page dots in status bar (wilidoro theme picker shape).
Confirm — modal question over content region: GREEN=yes, RED=no, GRAY=cancel/back; blocks and returns.
Spinner (ValueEditor) — bounded number/enum edit: YELLOW/BLUE dec/inc with repeat, GREEN accept, GRAY cancel.
Toast — 2 s transient one-liner above the rail; queued, never stacks.
BigStat — one scale-6+ value with caption for timer/score screens (wilidoro countdown shape).
LED echo — mirrors the rail onto WS2812 LEDs 1..5 (slot color at low brightness when bound, off when not); LEDs 0 and 6 stay app-owned (progress ring ends).
Chimes — three stock I2S cues wired into the framework: tick (press), rise (long-threshold), buzz (unbound key pressed).
proposals.exitStory: Two invariants make "stuck" impossible. (1) WHERE AM I: the framework draws the status bar on every screen — title plus one breadcrumb dot per stack level — and apps cannot suppress it outside declared game-mode. (2) HOW DO I LEAVE: GRAY is the system key and apps cannot bind it. Its rail slot always reads "Back" (or "Exit" at root); pressing it pops one level; at root it exits to App Explorer. Holding it 1 s exits to App Explorer from ANY depth — and this interception happens in the framework's input layer below the app, so even a fullscreen game that opted out of the rail still yields to gray-hold, with the "Home…" pill overlaid while it fills. The orca-field-notes incident ("how do i close this, im stuck") becomes structurally impossible: the answer is printed on-screen above the leftmost button on every screen of every app, and the one-sentence manual for the whole device is "Gray always takes you back."
proposals.resourcePlan: Framework is built on lcd_text + the graphics LCD API, NOT LVGL. LVGL costs ~390 KB flash + 143 KB of the display CPU's 264 KB RAM — over half of RAM for widgets a 5-slot rail doesn't need. Budget for fwog_ui: <=25 KB flash (font tables + rail/list/spinner/confirm/toast logic) and <=20 KB RAM: one full-width strip buffer (~15 KB per lcd_text.h's own numbers) reused for status bar, rail, and content lines, plus ~2 KB of screen-stack and key-state. No full framebuffer (320x240x2 = 150 KB, off the table). That keeps a typical app near the bare-app ~32 KB baseline and leaves >200 KB RAM for the feature itself. LVGL stays in the BSP as an opt-in for showcase apps (ogvegas), but its keypad map must be rebound to match the grammar — the current gray=UP/red=DOWN mapping directly contradicts gray=Back and is a consistency landmine; ship a fwog_ui-conformant LVGL group map alongside.
risks: Physical-layout assumption: the whole rail depends on buttons being a single row under the screen in gray..red order. If the case puts them beside the screen or reorders them, slot-to-button alignment lies to the user. Verify the case before freezing rail geometry.

Existing LVGL keypad map (gray=UP, green=ENTER, red=DOWN) contradicts the grammar (gray=Back). Any app shipped on the old map creates a second dialect; the BSP map must be migrated or every LVGL app breaks the gray guarantee.

5-char labels: some verbs and any localization won't fit; needs an abbreviation convention or a small icon set as fallback, or labels degrade into cryptic stubs and the 'labels are the manual' promise erodes.

RED contextual press vs 6 s shutdown: a user mashing/holding red in a hectic app (a game) can drift into power-off territory. The 1.5 s swallow + warning pill mitigates but does not eliminate accidental shutdowns.
Game-mode opt-out: apps that take the raw framebuffer lose the rail; the gray-hold intercept preserves escape but not discoverability. If too many apps opt out, the grammar stops being learned.

Color-blind and low-light use: color identity must stay secondary to position + text label. Any component that signals by color alone (LED echo, red=destructive) needs the label carrying the same information.
Two-key scrolling (yellow/blue + repeat) is slow on long lists (>100 items); may need long-press page-jump or first-letter index before a big content app ships.

Framework input interception below the app is a privileged path; a bug there (missed release, stuck repeat) bricks input for every app at once — it needs the same host-injected state-machine tests the debouncer already has.
proposals.pitch: CHROMABAR turns the five colored buttons from a constraint into the interface: every screen labels the physical buttons in their own colors on a rail aligned to the hardware, so the manual is printed on the screen at all times and a first-time user navigates by reading five words. One reserved key — gray, always Back, hold for Home — makes getting stuck structurally impossible and gives the whole device a one-sentence instruction. For developers, a screen is a struct: five labeled callbacks and a draw function, with lists, editors, confirms, toasts, LED echo, and chimes stocked in the BSP — so 'fw new-app' to a polished, grammar-conformant 3-screen feature is an afternoon, not a UI project. And by building on the 6x8 strip renderer instead of LVGL, the whole system costs ~25 KB flash and ~20 KB RAM instead of 390/143, leaving the display CPU's memory for features — which was the entire point.

components: ui_statusbar — framework-owned 16px top strip: breadcrumb (App > Screen) left, battery/link glyphs right; app never touches it
ui_hintbar — framework-owned 24px bottom strip: five 64px color-keyed chips physically aligned with the buttons, auto-filled from the screen declaration; empty chip = button inert here
ui_list — vertical list, 6 rows x 32px, GRAY/BLUE move cursor (auto-repeat on hold), GREEN selects; cursor position mirrored on the 7-LED strip
ui_text — paged/scrolling read-only text (orca-field-notes use case); GRAY/BLUE page, GREEN optional 'more' action
ui_value — single number/choice editor: big scale-4 value, GRAY/BLUE decrement/increment with repeat, GREEN commits, RED cancels
ui_hero — app-drawn 320x200 content region (timers, gauges, animations) with framework-owned chrome; the wilidoro screen type
ui_dialog — modal confirm: question + GREEN=yes / RED=no chips; blocks inside ui_run, no app event plumbing
ui_toast — 2s transient message strip over the content region, paired with a confirm chime
ui_progress — horizontal bar widget that optionally mirrors to the 7 WS2812 LEDs as a progress ring
ui_legend — framework-owned overlay on LONG-GRAY: full breadcrumb path, every button's current meaning, 'RED backs out' reminder; the built-in 'where am I' answer
ui_fx — the non-screen feedback layer: per-press LED flash in the pressed button's color, confirm/deny/exit chime set via I2S, invalid-press low blip
proposals.exitStory: The framework owns the nav stack and the RED button, so no app can strand a user. Invariant: MASHING RED ALWAYS GETS YOU OUT. Each RED press pops one screen; at the app's root screen, RED raises the framework's exit dialog ("Exit wilidoro?" GREEN chip = yes); one more RED press in that dialog ALSO confirms exit (deliberate — a panicked masher escapes, and exiting to App Explorer is never destructive because ui_on_exit() saved state first). The current meaning of RED ("Back" vs "Exit") is always printed in the red hint chip above the physical red button. A user who is merely lost, not fleeing, holds GRAY ~800ms: the ui_legend overlay shows the full breadcrumb (App > Screen > Screen) and every button's current meaning. Beneath all of that sits the hardware guarantee: RED held 6s powers off regardless of firmware state, and the framework renders a "still holding: power off in 3..2..1" banner from the 3s mark so the reserved gesture is discoverable instead of surprising. The orca-field-notes incident becomes impossible: that app under this framework would have had 'Back' printed over the red button on every screen.
proposals.inputGrammar:
Color IS the meaning, fixed device-wide; only YELLOW is app-defined. Assumed physical order (single row under the screen, left-to-right = bitfield order GRAY YELLOW GREEN BLUE RED) — FLAGGED: the hint-bar alignment depends on it.

GLOBAL (framework-owned, apps cannot rebind):
- RED press = BACK, always. Pops one screen; at app root, opens the exit dialog. RED never does anything destructive without a dialog.
- RED hold: 0-6s belongs to hardware power-off (reserved). The framework parks NOTHING on long-RED; from ~3s of hold it paints a "release to cancel — power off in 3..2..1" banner so the reserved gesture is legible.
- GREEN press = SELECT / CONFIRM / YES, always. Green means go.
- GREEN long (800ms) = screen's secondary select (e.g. "open item options") if declared, else no-op with a low blip.
- GRAY press = PREV (cursor up / page back / value down). Hold = auto-repeat, 400ms delay then 7/s, from down_since_ms.
- BLUE press = NEXT (cursor down / page fwd / value up). Hold = same repeat.
- GRAY long (800ms, no repeat consumed) = LEGEND overlay: breadcrumb + live button meanings. The universal "where am I".

CONTEXTUAL (the one app slot):
- YELLOW press = the screen's declared verb; its label is force-rendered in the yellow hint chip (no label, no action — the framework refuses silent bindings).
- YELLOW long = optional second verb, shown in the legend overlay.

Every accepted press flashes the pressed button's color on the LED strip and (optionally) clicks; an inert press gives a low blip — feedback without looking at the screen.
proposals.pitch: This wins because it spends the device's scarcest resources — 264 KB of RAM and five buttons — on identity instead of overhead. A fixed color grammar (green=go, red=back, gray/blue=prev/next, yellow=the app's one verb) plus a hint bar physically aligned with the buttons means a person who has never seen the device reads the screen once and knows every control, in every app, forever; the framework-owned nav stack makes "mash red to leave" a hardware-grade guarantee, so nobody is ever stuck again. Developers declare screens as static structs — a working 3-screen feature is ~25 lines with zero pixel math and zero event plumbing — so features ship at the speed of filling in a form. And by building a ~20 KB widget kit on the lcd_text/st7789 APIs already in the BSP instead of defaulting to LVGL's 143 KB RAM tax, apps keep ~115 KB more RAM for what actually differentiates them: audio, LEDs, sensors, and ideas. The screen never carries the UX alone — LEDs mirror position and progress, chimes confirm and deny — which is exactly what a 5-button, 7-LED, speaker-equipped handheld should feel like: not a phone with too few buttons, but an instrument.
proposals.resourcePlan: VERDICT: bespoke kit as the default template, LVGL demoted to opt-in for showcase apps. Numbers: LVGL costs ~390 KB flash + 143 KB of 264 KB RAM, leaving ~121 KB for app + I2S audio buffers + LED/IR/sensor state — wilidoro-class apps (audio + LEDs + IMU) are already squeezed, and every future app pays the tax whether it uses widgets or not. The bespoke 'wiliui' kit builds on what the BSP already ships (6x8 scalable font, padded text draw, windowed DMA blits, debounced buttons with down_since_ms): estimated ~18-22 KB flash, ~2 KB static RAM (nav stack of 8 screen pointers + chrome state), plus one optional 20 KB row buffer (320x32 RGB565) for flicker-free list-row redraws — total worst case ~24 KB RAM, i.e. ~119 KB RAM returned to apps vs LVGL. Frame latency at the ST7789's SPI rate (~62.5 MHz): full-screen push is 320x240x16b ≈ 1.23 Mb ≈ 20 ms (used only on screen transitions); steady-state updates are dirty rows — one 32px list row ≈ 20 KB ≈ 2.6 ms, a scale-4 value repaint ≈ 1 ms — so cursor movement tracks the 7/s auto-repeat with headroom and UI_HERO apps can hold 30+ fps on partial redraws. No full framebuffer exists or is needed. LVGL stays in the BSP (ogvegas keeps it; the existing keypad indev gets remapped to the grammar — RED→LV_KEY_ESC — so even LVGL apps obey 'red backs out'). Hybrid, with the cheap path as the paved one: 'fw new-app' scaffolds wiliui, and choosing LVGL is an explicit line in CMake with the RAM price in a comment next to it.
risks: Physical-layout assumption: hint-bar/button alignment presumes one row, left-to-right GRAY YELLOW GREEN BLUE RED under the screen. If the case differs (two rows, side-mounted, different order), the strongest learnability feature inverts into active harm. Verify against real hardware before freezing hintbar geometry; the chip order is one table in ui_hintbar.

LONG-RED adjacency: exit lives on red-mash, power-off on red-hold-6s. A panicked user who holds instead of mashes sails toward power-off; the 3s on-screen countdown mitigates but only if they are looking at the screen. Tune the exit dialog to appear fast (<150ms) so mashing visibly works before holding is tried.

Grammar schism with the existing LVGL keypad map (gray=UP, red=DOWN, blue=RIGHT): shipped LVGL apps use red as a navigation key, new grammar makes red=back. Until the indev map is patched and ogvegas/lvgl-demo rebuilt, the device speaks two dialects — worst possible outcome for a consistency play. Patch the LVGL keypad map in the same release the framework lands.

Red/green = no/yes parks meaning on hue: ~4% of users are red-green colorblind. Position (red rightmost), text labels in every chip, and X/check glyphs must carry the meaning redundantly — treat as a launch requirement, not polish.

No framebuffer means transitions are visible paints (~20 ms top-to-bottom); acceptable, but UI_HERO apps doing naive full-screen clears every tick will flicker. The API pushes dirty-region habits (ui_dirty, row buffer) but cannot force them in render() callbacks — document loudly in the template.

Component-kit scope creep: the moment someone asks for tables, tabs, or a grid, the 20 KB kit starts its march toward being a worse LVGL. Hold the line at the 11 listed components; anything richer is the signal that THAT app should pay the LVGL tax instead.

ui_confirm blocking inside ui_run is simple for devs but wrong for apps with hard real-time side work (audio streaming during a dialog); those apps need the on_tick path kept alive during modals — make the modal pump tick_ms callbacks or wilidoro-class apps will stutter.
proposals.screenAnatomy:
320x240 landscape, three fixed horizontal bands (framework-owned chrome top and bottom, app content between):

1. STATUS BAR — y 0-15, 320x16px. Left: breadcrumb at scale-2 text (12x16 glyphs, ~26 chars max, middle-truncated: "wilidoro>Set>Bright"). Right: up to 4 status glyphs (battery, link, IR, mute) at 12px, right-aligned in 56px. Inverse-video strip (fg/bg swapped) so it reads as chrome, not content.

2. CONTENT REGION — y 16-215, 320x200px. All app pixels live here and only here. Stock layouts inside it: UI_LIST = 6 rows of 32px (24px scale-3 text + 8px padding, cursor row inverse-video, optional 16px color chip at x 0-15); UI_TEXT = scale-2 text, 26 cols x 12 lines; UI_VALUE = scale-4 label (24x32 glyphs) centered with prev/next arrows; UI_HERO = raw 320x200 handed to the app's render(). Overlays (dialog/toast/legend) paint inside this band and force a band repaint on dismiss — chrome is never damaged.

3. HINT BAR — y 216-239, 320x24px. Five 64px-wide chips, one per physical button in bitfield order (GRAY|YELLOW|GREEN|BLUE|RED — the flagged alignment assumption). Each chip: 4px underline in the button's color across its full 64px, label above it at scale-1 (6x8, max 10 chars, centered). Empty label = dimmed underline only = button inert on this screen. This bar is the manual: the device documents itself on every screen for 24px of the 240.
proposals.stanceName: The 20 KB Color Grammar — bespoke-first hybrid (wiliui over lcd_text; LVGL opt-in, never default)
DECK — a declarative screen-graph UI framework (dev-velocity first: declare screens as const data, the grammar falls out)
proposals.inputGrammar:
Hardware bitfield order GRAY, YELLOW, GREEN, BLUE, RED is also the assumed physical left-to-right row under the screen (FLAGGED ASSUMPTION — the hint bar aligns chips to buttons positionally).

GLOBAL (framework-enforced, identical in every app):
- GRAY = PREV/UP. Press: selection up / scroll up / decrement field. Auto-repeat: after 400 ms, every 80 ms (uses fwog_btn_held_ms).
- YELLOW = NEXT/DOWN. Exact mirror of GRAY. The adjacent left pair reads as a rocker.
- GREEN = YES/SELECT. Press: activate row, enter/commit field, confirm dialog, dismiss toast. Long-press (600 ms): screen's declared long action only (e.g. save-all on a form); no declaration = ignored.
- RED = OUT, and only OUT. Press: back (pop nav stack); at app root: opens Exit-to-Explorer dialog. Hold 1.5 s: same exit dialog from ANY depth, non-suppressible, with an on-screen countdown ring starting at 500 ms so the user sees the escalation. Hold ~6 s: hardware power-off (reserved, untouched — the ladder back < exit < power-off means holding RED always escalates toward "more out", never collides). RED never repeats, never scrolls, is never a gameplay verb. CANVAS screens may claim short-press RED only by declaring owns_back (hint chip then shows their meaning); the 1.5 s hold is never claimable.

CONTEXTUAL (exactly one button):
- BLUE = THE APP BUTTON. Press: the screen's one declared verb (pause, shuffle, next-tab). Long-press (600 ms): declared overflow menu, else nothing. Its hint chip always names the current meaning; an empty chip means it does nothing here. This is the only button whose meaning moves, and it is always labeled.

Dialogs: GREEN = yes, RED = no — same colors as everywhere. Repeat exists only on GRAY/YELLOW. This replaces the LVGL keypad map (red=DOWN is banned: it puts a scroll key on the power ladder); the LVGL port's keymap gets patched to gray=PREV, yellow=NEXT, green=ENTER, blue=custom, red=ESC so both stacks speak one grammar.
proposals.screenAnatomy:
320x240 landscape, three fixed bands, no framebuffer (windowed lcd_text/rect blits):

- STATUS BAR: y 0–19 (320x20). App name left (scale-2, 12x16 glyphs, max 10 chars), screen title center (max 12 chars, ellipsized), right cluster: breadcrumb depth dots (one 4px dot per nav level, max 6) + battery glyph. Framework-drawn, apps never touch it.
- CONTENT: y 20–215 (320x196). Owned by the screen kind: LIST/FORM = 8 rows of 24 px (scale-2 text, 25 cols), rightmost 6 px reserved for scroll ticks; DETAIL = 8 wrapped scale-2 lines, page "2/5" rendered into status-bar right; PROGRESS = title line + scale-4 value (24x32 digits) + 280x16 bar centered; CANVAS = raw 320x196 unless FWOG_UI_FULLSCREEN.
- HINT BAR: y 216–239 (320x24). Five 64x24 chips in hardware order GRAY|YELLOW|GREEN|BLUE|RED, positionally over/under the physical buttons (the flagged assumption). Each chip: 4 px band in the button's actual color across the top, then scale-1 text (6x8), max 10 chars, centered. Auto-derived from the screen declaration — devs never write hints.
- OVERLAYS: dialog 280x120 centered with 2 px border (GREEN/RED chips relabel to Yes/No beneath it); toast 300x28 bottom-anchored above the hint bar, 2 s auto-dismiss.
FULLSCREEN canvases still get the hint bar flashed for 1.5 s on entry and the RED hold-countdown ring drawn over their pixels.
components: StatusBar — automatic app/title/depth/battery strip; the permanent answer to "where am I".
HintBar — five color-matched chips auto-generated from the screen declaration; the permanent answer to "what do the buttons do".
List — scrolling menu of label(+optional value) rows, wrap-around, scroll ticks, on_pick(index) callback.
Detail — word-wrapped text pages fed by a get_line/get_text callback; GRAY/YELLOW page, auto page indicator.
Form — array of fields (INT with min/max/step, BOOL, ENUM of strings) bound to app variables by pointer; GRAY/YELLOW adjust, GREEN advances/commits, on_commit callback.
Progress — get_pct callback polled at 10 Hz, big numeral + bar, auto-mirrored to the 7-LED WS2812 strip, on_done callback; BLUE verb slot for skip/pause.
Dialog — modal GREEN/RED confirm; the framework's own exit dialog is this same component.
Toast — fwog_ui_toast(msg): 2 s transient banner, GREEN dismisses early.
Canvas — draw(dirty) + on_btn(event) escape hatch for games/visualizers; framework keeps bars unless FWOG_UI_FULLSCREEN and always keeps RED-hold.
FeedbackMap — semantic chime+LED events fired automatically (select tick, page turn, error buzz, exit chirp) via I2S + WS2812, overridable per app theme, so sound/light consistency comes free too.
proposals.exitStory: Three guarantees the app cannot break. (1) The status bar is always present (fullscreen canvases excepted) showing app name, screen title, and one breadcrumb dot per stack level — "where am I" is literally printed. (2) The RED hint chip always reads "Back", or "Exit" at the root — the way out is labeled in the button's own color, positioned over the physical button. (3) The escalation ladder is muscle memory: tap RED repeatedly and you always reach root then the "Exit to Explorer?" dialog; or hold RED 1.5 s from anywhere — including inside a fullscreen game — and the framework (not the app) draws a countdown ring, raises the exit dialog, and on GREEN reboots into App Explorer via the FwOGapp contract. Keep holding and the existing 6 s hardware power-off fires, so even a frozen app yields. The orca-field-notes "I'm stuck" failure becomes impossible in any DECK app because exit lives in the library, above app code, and owns_back canvases can only claim the short press, never the hold.
proposals.resourcePlan: DECK is built on lcd_text + the st7789 rect/window primitives — NOT on LVGL. Numbers force it: LVGL costs ~390 KB flash and 143 KB of the display CPU's 264 KB RAM, leaving apps ~120 KB; the bare display stack is ~32 KB. DECK adds five fixed-layout widgets over lcd_text, needing no framebuffer (per-glyph windowed blits, ~1 KB glyph scratch at scale 4). Budget: framework ≤ 48 KB flash including the 6x8 font and chime samples' index, ≤ 8 KB static RAM (nav stack depth 8, hint strings, dialog state, LED mirror) — screens themselves are const structs in flash, costing app RAM nothing. The LVGL port stays in the BSP as an opt-in for showcase apps (ogvegas-class) that genuinely need styled graphics, with its keymap patched to the DECK grammar so the two stacks feel identical; the 'fw new-app' template links DECK by default and never LVGL. lcd_text's 95-glyph ASCII font is the accepted ceiling (no unicode).
risks: Physical-layout assumption: the hint bar's whole learnability trick assumes the five buttons sit in one GRAY..RED row directly below/beside the screen; if the case arranges them otherwise (column, split), chip placement must be re-mapped before the grammar ships. Verify on the actual case first.

RED ladder timing: a panicked user holding RED sails from exit-dialog (1.5 s) into power-off (6 s); the countdown ring mitigates but needs on-device testing with real users, and the 1.5 s threshold must stay far from both debounce and 6 s.

Grammar migration: the existing LVGL keypad map (red=DOWN) contradicts DECK; until the LVGL keymap patch and reference apps (lvgl demo, orca) are converted, two grammars coexist and confuse exactly the users this fixes.

Canvas escape hatch erosion: every app that finds the five kinds limiting will reach for CANVAS and re-invent inconsistent UI; hold the line by growing the kind list deliberately (max ~7) rather than adding per-screen style knobs.

Declarative struct sprawl: designated-init macros hide a tagged union that will attract optional fields; each new option taxes every app's flash and the docs — require two real apps needing a feature before it lands.

ASCII-only 6x8 font: no i18n, limited glyph legibility at scale 1 in the hint chips (10 chars); acceptable for now, but hint wording needs a style guide (verbs, <=10 chars) or chips degrade into cryptic abbreviations.

Framework must coexist with the default power policy's RED handling — double-handling the 6 s hold (framework exit dialog re-arming it, or eating the event) would break the one reserved semantic; needs an explicit shared ownership test in the BSP suite.
proposals.pitch: DECK wins because it sells the 5-button constraint as the product: five colors, five permanent meanings — gray/yellow rock through anything, green always says yes, blue is the app's one labeled verb, red always gets you out and only ever escalates toward out, gracefully ending at the hardware's own 6-second power-off. A developer declares screens as const data — list, detail, form, progress, canvas — and a complete 3-screen feature is under 30 lines with navigation, status bar, color-matched hint chips, LED mirroring, chimes, and a non-suppressible exit ladder all inherited from the library; there is no way to build a DECK app in which a user can get stuck, because \"where am I and how do I leave\" is rendered by framework code the app cannot reach. And it fits the machine: built on the BSP's existing lcd_text and button phase engine at ~48 KB flash / 8 KB RAM instead of LVGL's 143 KB RAM tax, it leaves the 264 KB display CPU to the feature — which is exactly the owner's brief: crank out features, get the UI for free.

One Color, One Verb — a fixed global grammar where each button is a word learned once
The 20 KB Color Grammar — bespoke-first hybrid (wiliui over lcd_text; LVGL opt-in, never default)
CHROMABAR — soft-key rail with a hard gray guarantee
verdicts.scores:
DECK — LOC: 9 (27-line complete app; screens are const flash data; the Form widget with pointer-bound INT/BOOL/ENUM fields makes settings screens near-zero code, the single biggest velocity multiplier of any proposal). Accidental-violation resistance: 9 (exactly one contextual button, BLUE, and it cannot act without a label; hint chips auto-derived so devs literally never write hints). API-prevents-inconsistency: 9 (five screen kinds cover the real app fleet; canvas is the only leak and owns_back can claim only the short press, never the hold). Stuck-impossible: 9 (RED escalation ladder back < exit < power-off lives in library code above the app; 1.5s hold non-suppressible even fullscreen).
One Color, One Verb — LOC: 8 (~30 lines; constructor-per-kind is clean but no multi-field form, so a settings screen with 3 values = 3 pushes). Accidental-violation resistance: 10 (the event enum is the whole app surface — GRAY/RED/nav events never reach app code, so a dev cannot rebind navigation even on purpose). API-prevents-inconsistency: 8 (one long-GREEN slot is watertight but so tight that real apps will flee to Canvas, its own #1 risk — consistency by starvation erodes). Stuck-impossible: 9 (RED pops everywhere including canvas; GRAY overlay with breadcrumb + explicit exit item is a second labeled path).
The 20 KB Color Grammar (wiliui) — LOC: 9 (~25 lines, flat declarative structs, framework refuses unlabeled yellow bindings). Accidental-violation resistance: 8 (one YELLOW verb + optional long, force-labeled; UI_HERO hands apps 320x200 raw with no lint on what they draw). API-prevents-inconsistency: 8 (same declared-kind model as DECK, slightly weaker: flat struct with per-kind dead fields invites misuse, blocking ui_confirm starves on_tick). Stuck-impossible: 9 (mash-RED invariant plus RED-also-confirms-exit-dialog means a panicking masher escapes; ui_on_exit save hook makes exit never destructive).
CHROMABAR — LOC: 7 (compact example, but custom screens need a hand-written 5-slot key table + draw callback — more decisions per screen than declaring a kind). Accidental-violation resistance: 5 (yellow/blue/green/red are all per-screen rebindable; 'green is primary by convention' is a hope, not an API constraint — dialect drift is designed in). API-prevents-inconsistency: 6 (labels are forced, which helps, but forced labels on inconsistent meanings just documents the inconsistency). Stuck-impossible: 10 (best exit in the field: GRAY press = back unbindable, GRAY-hold intercepted in the input layer below the app, works even in raw-framebuffer game mode).
Color-Coded Compass — LOC: 8 (~30 declarative lines riding mature LVGL widgets). Accidental-violation resistance: 4 (fwui_add_* returns raw lv_obj_t, handing every app the full LVGL styling API — the design system becomes advisory the day someone calls lv_obj_set_style). API-prevents-inconsistency: 5 (widgets are consistent but fwui_hint allows arbitrary PRESS remaps, and the LVGL escape hatch is wide open). Stuck-impossible: 4 (the only back/exit is LONG-YELLOW, a hidden 700ms gesture — precisely the class of invisible affordance that produced the orca incident; plus chrome dies if the app busy-loops, acknowledged unfixed in v1; plus RED=DOWN with 20Hz auto-repeat parks a scroll key on the 6s power-off button).
grafts: CHROMABAR's below-the-app GRAY-hold interception: the framework input layer swallows gray-hold and exits to App Explorer even from a raw-framebuffer game that opted out of all chrome — DECK's RED ladder should be enforced at this same layer, not in the widget loop, so a busy-looping or canvas app can never starve the escape path.

CHROMABAR's long-press teaching feedback: at the long threshold the chip fills solid in the button's color showing the long-label plus a chime, so users learn long-press meanings safely by accident — apply to DECK's GREEN-long and BLUE-long slots.
Compass's accelerating auto-repeat (8 Hz after 500 ms, 20 Hz after 2 s) on the GRAY/YELLOW rocker — without it, 200-item lists are a 6-second hold and someone will demand a grammar exception.

wiliui's panic-masher clause: RED inside the exit dialog also confirms exit, paired with the ui_on_exit(save_state) hook so exiting is never destructive — mashing red from any depth lands in App Explorer with state saved.

One Verb's GRAY system overlay: full breadcrumb path, app-registered menu items, and an explicit labeled 'Exit to App Explorer' row — a second, spelled-out exit path for users who read instead of mash.

wiliui's eyes-free feedback pair: every accepted press flashes the pressed button's color on the LED strip, every inert press gives a low blip — confirmation without looking, ideal for one-handed use.

The LVGL keymap patch (proposed by CHROMABAR, DECK, and wiliui alike): rebind the BSP's LVGL keypad indev to the winning grammar (red→LV_KEY_ESC etc.) in the same release the framework lands, so opt-in LVGL showcase apps speak the same dialect instead of teaching a second one.

Power-off legibility (all four bespoke proposals converge): from ~2-3 s of RED hold the framework paints a 'release to cancel — power off in 3..2..1' countdown, turning the reserved 6 s hardware semantic into a visible feature instead of a trap.
fatalFlaws: Compass's promotion of the existing LVGL keypad map to a contract puts RED=DOWN with 20 Hz auto-repeat on the same button as the 6-second hardware power-off: a user holding scroll-down in a long list is literally driving toward shutdown. A scroll key must never live on the power ladder.

Compass's only back/exit affordance is LONG-YELLOW, a 700 ms hidden gesture with no press-level Back anywhere — this reproduces the exact discoverability failure ('how do i close orca field notes') the system exists to kill. Every shipped grammar needs a plain-press Back.

Compass's fwui_add_* functions returning raw lv_obj_t handles give every app the full LVGL styling/positioning API — the design system is unenforceable the moment the first dev calls into LVGL directly. If LVGL is ever used underneath, the handles must stay opaque.

Mandatory LVGL as the default framework backend (143 KB of the display CPU's 264 KB RAM, per Compass's plan) must not ship: a framework that spends 54% of RAM before the app draws forbids exactly the audio/LED/sensor feature work the brief demands. LVGL stays opt-in for showcase apps only.

CHROMABAR's free per-screen rebinding of YELLOW/BLUE/GREEN/RED (only GRAY reserved) must not ship as-is: with four of five buttons app-definable per screen, the 'one grammar across all apps' promise dissolves into per-app dialects with pretty labels. Cap the contextual budget at one labeled verb button (DECK's BLUE) — the rest are fixed words.

wiliui's blocking ui_confirm inside ui_run starves on_tick during modals (its own risk list admits wilidoro-class audio apps will stutter): modals must keep pumping tick callbacks before this API freezes.

Universal invariant no proposal may weaken: nothing is ever bindable on LONG-RED and the 6 s hardware power-off is never suppressed or double-handled — the framework may only overlay a countdown, and this shared-ownership contract with the default power policy needs an explicit BSP test.

CHROMABAR — soft-key rail with a hard gray guarantee
The 20 KB Color Grammar — bespoke-first hybrid (wiliui over lcd_text; LVGL opt-in, never default)
DECK — a declarative screen-graph UI framework (dev-velocity first: declare screens as const data, the grammar falls out)
verdicts.scores:
Criteria: list-nav / go-back / find-home / stuck-exit / power-off / no-accidental-destruction (1-10, first-contact only).

ONE COLOR ONE VERB: 8/10/10/10/8/9. List: yellow-blue flanking green reads as prev-OK-next, legend keycaps in button colors. Back: RED press = back matches the universal red=stop instinct AND is labeled — the panic press is the correct press. Home: mashing red bottoms out in App Explorer with no dialog trap; gray overlay redundantly lists Exit. Stuck: nav events never reach app code, gray/red owned even on canvas. Power: countdown from 2s, earliest meaningful warning; panic-hold does drift to off, but off is 'more out'. Destruction: only app slot is a labeled long-green; red is never delete.

CHROMABAR: 8/8/9/10/9/8. List: same flanking pair, rail labels aligned to buttons. Back: gray-press works and is always labeled, but it is counter-instinct — a no-manual user presses red first and gets a contextual verb; back requires reading. Home: gray-mash to root then exit (optional dirty-confirm adds a step). Stuck: best in field — gray-hold intercepted in the input layer below the app, works in raw game mode, no dialog. Power: red swallowed past 1.5s with warning pill = lowest accidental-off risk of all five. Destruction: 'destructive family on red press' is the one instinct-press hazard.

20 KB COLOR GRAMMAR: 6/10/9/9/8/7. List: GRAY/BLUE are positions 1 and 4 — a non-adjacent vertical rocker with two other buttons between them; worst ergonomics on the single most common task. Back: red press, labeled, and RED-in-exit-dialog also confirms — the only masher-proof exit in the field. Home: red mash guaranteed; LONG-GRAY legend is good but supplemental (long-press discoverability is poor). Power: 3s banner fine. Destruction: yellow app verb has no mandated confirm — the proposal's own example binds factory_reset to a single press.

DECK: 7/9/7/8/8/8. List: gray/yellow adjacent rocker, hint chips fine. Back: red press, labeled, instinct-aligned. Home: exit dialog where RED = No — a panicked red-masher opens the dialog, cancels it, reopens it, forever; escape requires stopping to press green. Stuck: red-hold 1.5s non-suppressible is good, but canvases may claim short-press red (owns_back), eroding the one instinct users have. Power: coherent 'red only escalates toward out' ladder, ring from 500ms. Destruction: labeled blue verb, low risk.

COLOR-CODED COMPASS: 7/3/5/5/4/4. List: outer-vertical/inner-horizontal spatial map is elegant and matches the existing BSP. Everything else fails first contact: the ONLY back is LONG-YELLOW — an undiscoverable gesture advertised in 10px text inside a 60x20 chip; a first-timer pressing yellow gets LEFT. Exit is long-press into a dialog, or a LONG-GREEN menu — two hidden gestures. Fatally, RED = DOWN with accelerating hold-to-repeat parks routine list scrolling directly on the 6-second hardware power-off ladder: a first-timer holding 'down' through a 200-item list shuts the device off. The proposal admits both problems in its own risks.
grafts: From 20 KB Color Grammar: RED pressed inside the framework's exit dialog ALSO confirms exit — a panicked masher must escape, never loop (fixes the dialog-trap DECK has and hardens the winner's root-exit).
From 20 KB Color Grammar: the LONG-GRAY legend overlay — full breadcrumb plus every button's current meaning — as the universal 'where am I' answer layered on top of the winner's gray system overlay.
From 20 KB Color Grammar: non-visual feedback contract — accepted press flashes the pressed button's color on the LED strip, inert press gives a low blip — feedback without looking at the screen.

From CHROMABAR: input-layer interception BELOW app code so the system escape (gray/red) works even in raw-framebuffer game mode, with the filling 'Home…' pill; escape must not depend on the app's event loop.
From CHROMABAR: at the long-press threshold the key's on-screen slot fills with the button's color and shows the long-label plus a chime — users learn long-press meanings by accident, safely.
From CHROMABAR: unbound buttons render a dim dot — silence is also labeled, so a first-timer never wonders whether a dead button is broken.
From DECK: the explicit escalation-ladder framing and early countdown ring on RED holds (back < exit < power-off, visualized from ~500ms) so holding red is always legible as 'more out'.

From Color-Coded Compass: accelerating auto-repeat on the nav pair (8Hz rising to ~20Hz) so long lists are usable with two buttons — but NEVER on RED; and its risk-list idea of a display-CPU watchdog that paints 'unresponsive — hold RED to power off' when an app busy-loops.

From CHROMABAR/DECK resource stance (shared by the winner): ship the bespoke <=32KB-flash/<=10KB-RAM kit as the 'fw new-app' default, keep LVGL opt-in, and patch the LVGL keypad map (red -> ESC/back) in the SAME release so the fleet speaks one grammar.
fatalFlaws: Color-Coded Compass: LONG-YELLOW as the only back gesture must not ship — a hidden long-press advertised in 10px chip text is undiscoverable to a first-time user; the observed 'stuck in orca field notes' failure recurs on day one.

Color-Coded Compass: RED = DOWN with hold-to-repeat must not ship — it parks the most-used navigation verb on the 6-second hardware power-off ladder; a first-timer scrolling a long list by holding 'down' powers the device off mid-use. The brief explicitly warned against colliding with the RED-hold shutdown contract.

DECK: an exit dialog where RED = No, reached by mashing RED, must not ship as-is — the panic gesture opens and cancels the dialog in a loop and the user never exits; RED in that dialog must confirm (graft #1) or root-exit must be direct.

DECK: owns_back canvases claiming short-press RED must not ship without tighter limits — it hands apps the one button first-timers instinctively press to escape, recreating per-app dialects exactly where consistency matters most.
CHROMABAR: 'destructive family on RED single press' must not ship without a mandatory Confirm — the instinct panic-press for a no-manual user is RED, and it must never delete anything.

20 KB Color Grammar: the API example binding factory_reset to a single unconfirmed YELLOW press must not ship — any destructive verb on the app slot must route through the Confirm dialog; forced labels are not sufficient protection for a first-time user.

All proposals: shipping the new grammar while the existing LVGL keypad map (gray=UP, red=DOWN) remains in reference apps must not happen — two contradictory dialects on one device is worse for first-contact learnability than either alone; the LVGL map patch and reference-app migration land in the same release as the framework.

Any proposal freezing hint-bar/rail geometry before verifying the physical case layout — every design's core learnability mechanism (on-screen labels positionally aligned to physical buttons) inverts into active harm if the assumed single-row GRAY..RED order is wrong. Verify the case first; this is a ship blocker, not a footnote.

ranking: DECK — a declarative screen-graph UI framework (dev-velocity first: declare screens as const data, the grammar falls out)
The 20 KB Color Grammar — bespoke-first hybrid (wiliui over lcd_text; LVGL opt-in, never default)
CHROMABAR — soft-key rail with a hard gray guarantee
One Color, One Verb — a fixed global grammar where each button is a word learned once
verdicts.scores: DECK: resource-honesty 9 (≤48KB flash/≤8KB RAM over lcd_text, per-glyph blit scratch matches lcd_text.h's own 96*scale^2 numbers, const screens live in flash costing zero RAM); reserved-semantics 10 (RED never repeats, never a nav verb, and the back < exit-dialog < power-off ladder means holding RED only ever escalates toward 'more out' — the only proposal where the 6s hardware cutoff is grammatically coherent; also names the double-handling-with-power-policy test as a risk); migration 7 (concrete same-stack plan: patch LVGL keymap to red=ESC, but yellow LEFT→NEXT still retrains all four apps); maintainability 9 (screens as const tagged-union data is the most reviewable C11 shape; struct-sprawl risk self-identified with a two-app rule). | 20KB Color Grammar: resource-honesty 10 (the only proposal that did the actual physics — 62.5MHz SPI, 20ms full push, 2.6ms dirty row vs 7/s repeat, 24KB worst-case RAM — and it checks out against the BSP); reserved-semantics 9 (nothing parked on long-RED, 3s countdown banner, RED-in-dialog-confirms is safe only because ui_on_exit saves first); migration 8 (most explicit plan: RED→LV_KEY_ESC indev patch shipped in the same release, per-app disposition named); maintainability 8 (clean flat API, but blocking ui_confirm stalling on_tick is a real hazard given audio lives on this CPU — at least it flagged it). | CHROMABAR: resource-honesty 9 (25KB/20KB budget cites lcd_text.h's 15KB strip figure, which is literally in the file — verified); reserved-semantics 8 (LONG-RED unbindable, 1.5s swallow+pill, but 'swallows the event' needs the shared-ownership test with the default power policy it doesn't name, and per-app contextual RED press near the power ladder is looser than DECK's fixed RED=OUT); migration 7 (names the keymap landmine, ships a conformant LVGL group map, but gray=Back inverts gray=UP for all four apps); maintainability 8 (screen-as-struct-of-callbacks is fine C11; privileged input-intercept layer is a single point of failure it honestly flags). | One Color One Verb: resource-honesty 8 (24-32KB/≤10KB plausible on the same lcd_text substrate, less arithmetic shown); reserved-semantics 9 (nothing on long-RED, 2s countdown, RED=BACK everywhere); migration 6 (lists the two-dialect fleet as debt but has no concrete patch plan or sequencing — weakest migration story of the bespoke four); ~120KB headroom is not free money); reserved-semantics 2 (RED=DOWN with hold-to-repeat parks the single most frequent navigation gesture on the power-off button: scrolling a 200-item list at its own stated 8→20Hz curve takes ~9.4s of continuous RED hold, sailing past the 6s hardware cutoff — the device powers off mid-scroll, countdown toast or not); migration 10 (zero cost — promotes the existing keypad map to contract, all four apps already conform); maintainability 7 (thin 15KB layer over upstream-maintained LVGL is genuinely low-maintenance C, and it alone flagged the CPU-split question — which the BSP answers: app UI and audio share the display CPU).
grafts: From 20KB Color Grammar: the frame-latency budget discipline — dirty-row repaints (~2.6ms/row, ~1ms value repaint) sized against the repeat rate, and the explicit rule that full-screen pushes (~20ms) happen only on transitions. The final system should ship these numbers in the framework docs as a contract, not folklore.

From 20KB Color Grammar: modals must keep pumping on_tick — audio/LED/sensor drivers live on the display CPU (bsp/display_cpu/{audio,leds,sensors}), so a blocking confirm that stops the tick loop will stutter wilidoro-class apps. Make the modal pump a launch requirement, not a flagged risk.
From Color-Coded Compass: accelerating auto-repeat (8Hz → 20Hz after 2s) so long lists never need multi-second holds — but grafted onto safe keys only (the prev/next pair), never RED.
From CHROMABAR: long-press pedagogy — at the long threshold the hint chip fills with the button's color, shows the long label, and chimes, so users learn long-press meanings by accident, safely.

From CHROMABAR: the escape intercept living in the framework's input layer BELOW the app, so even a raw-framebuffer game yields to the exit hold with an on-screen fill indicator; combine with DECK's rule that canvases may claim short-press only, never the hold.
From CHROMABAR: the unbound-slot dim-dot convention — silence is also labeled, so an inert button is visibly inert rather than mysteriously dead.

From One Color One Verb: the IMU-tilt escape valve for games needing more axes than the fixed grammar grants (wilidoro's tilt-to-pause already proves it on this hardware) — relieves the pressure to grant grammar exemptions.

From One Color One Verb / CHROMABAR: force-labeled contextual bindings — the framework refuses to bind an app verb without a hint-chip label ('the chip is the license to remap'); no silent bindings, ever.

From Color-Coded Compass: the display-CPU watchdog idea — a hung app gets an 'unresponsive — hold RED to power off' banner painted by something below the app. Pairs naturally with DECK's non-suppressible RED hold.

From CHROMABAR/DECK: semantic feedback events (select tick, error buzz, exit chirp on I2S; LED flash in the pressed button's color) wired into the framework so sound/light consistency is inherited, not reimplemented per app.

From all four bespoke proposals: the power-off countdown banner from ~3s of RED hold, so the reserved 6s hardware cutoff is announced rather than mysterious — this survives regardless of which grammar ships.
fatalFlaws: Compass's RED=DOWN with hold-to-repeat must NOT ship: by its own timing (500ms delay, 8Hz, 20Hz after 2s), scrolling ~190 items requires holding RED past the 6-second hardware power-off — the device shuts down mid-scroll. No countdown toast fixes a grammar that makes routine navigation and power-off the same physical gesture; the reserved semantic is non-negotiable per the FwOGapp contract.

Compass's resource premise 'the display CPU's entire job is UI, so spending its RAM on UI is the correct allocation' must not survive into any rationale: the BSP tree (bsp/display_cpu/) puts audio, LEDs, IR, sensors, and power management on the display CPU. LVGL's 143KB is not competing with nothing — it competes with I2S buffers, LED state, and sensor processing on a 264KB part. LVGL-as-mandatory-default must not ship; LVGL-as-opt-in (which all four other proposals converge on) is the correct disposition.

CHROMABAR's 'swallows the event until hardware cuts power' RED handling must not ship as written: the framework sitting between the driver and the default power policy risks starving or double-handling the 6s hold. DECK's risk list names the fix — an explicit shared-ownership test in the BSP suite for the RED-hold path — and that test must exist before any framework touches RED hold events.

Shipping any new grammar WITHOUT patching the LVGL keypad map (fwog_lvgl.c: gray=UP, red=DOWN) and rebuilding the reference apps in the same release must not happen: a fleet speaking two contradictory dialects is worse for learnability than either dialect alone (correctly identified by three proposals). The keymap patch and the framework are one atomic release, not a migration 'later'.

A blocking modal that halts the app tick loop (20KB Grammar's ui_confirm as sketched, CHROMABAR's blocking fwog_ui_confirm) must not ship on a CPU that also pumps I2S audio — modals must keep the tick/audio path alive or wilidoro-class apps audibly stutter during every confirm dialog.
